newsitem.title: CANADA: CANOLA--Canadian crush seen slowed by poor margins.
newsitem.headline: CANOLA--Canadian crush seen slowed by poor margins.

text.p: Canada's expanding canola crushing industry has been forced to slow its red-hot pace this autumn due to poor profit margins, but domestic processing may still set a record this season, analysts said.

"Even with the plant shutdowns there's probably a pretty good chance we'll match last year's record crush and maybe exceed it unless the crush margins keep dropping," Agriculture Canada oilseed analyst Lyndon Peters said.
Canola crushers won't reveal margins but profitability in recent weeks has eroded as competing soyproduct prices fell.
"Canola oil and meal storage is not a problem for Canbra," said Canbra Foods Ltd president Larry McNamara, who said the downtime resulted from negative crushing margins.
Canbra shut down its 1,000-tonne-a-day canola crush plant in Lethbridge, Alberta, three weeks ago.
McNamara said the plant would resume a limited production run in mid-November to meet a contract and then would remain shut until the spread between canola, soyoil and soymeal improves.

Compared to six weeks ago on September 13, Winnipeg Commodity Exchange November canola prices are down 9.4 percent while Chicago Board of Trade December soyoil has fallen 12.7 percent and December soymeal has fallen 11.8 percent.
Nevertheless, Peters and others expect the canola crush in the 1996/97 (August/July) season to total 2.8-3.0 million tonnes, compared to last year's record 2.75 million tonnes.
Canada's processors used 509,000 tonnes of canola in August-September, up 30 percent from 392,000 tonnes in the same period last year, according to the Canadian Oilseed Processors Association.
That active pace comes from a smaller crop this year, with Statistics Canada estimating canola output at 4.979 million tonnes, down 17 percent from 6.436 million a year earlier.
But both harvest and crush supplies have meant a seasonal downturn in prices and plant shutdowns this month.
"A shutdown was almost warranted because these guys were going so hot and heavy that I'm sure they were running out of storage space," James Richardson & Sons Ltd analyst David Champion said.
So far three of Canada's five canola processors have announced shutdowns.
To make crushing attractive, McNamara said, spot canola prices need to decline to C$380 a tonne while U.S. soyoil prices rise to 25 U.S. cents a pound and soymeal to US$240 a short ton.
WCE Nov canola ended at C$395.20 a tonne Wednesday, CBOT Dec soyoil at 22.94 cents/lb and Dec soymeal at $226.60 a ton.
Also citing poor margins, Cargill Ltd shut its new 2,000 tonne per day capacity canola crushing plant in Clavet, Saskatchewan, on Tuesday. CanAmera Foods said on October 11 it was scaling back.
A CanAmera spokesman cited the smaller canola crop, larger domestic crush capacity and vegetable oil import duties in Japan and Mexico as pressuring profit margins.
But analysts also said that as crusher demand for canola cools, export demand for canola was expected to rise.
Canadian exports of canola since August 1 were 512,000 tonnes as of October 20, down from 608,900 tonnes a year earlier.
Meanwhile, domestic disappearance over the same period was 623,200 tonnes, up from 500,300 tonnes last year.
(Winnipeg bureau 204 947 3548)
